wave1.coupling_tension: Three of the 2B marginals look internally inconsistent once 2A's demographics/fiscal block is endogenous, and the inconsistency is directional, not noise. (1) AI-Q3 (data-centre TWh, P50 998) was priced with demographics exogenous, i.e. with the cost of capital taken as given. My CQ4 reference-class answer puts the G7 10y real yield at a P50 of ~2.1% with a P90 of 3.4%, anchored on a ~2.0% starting level and on debt arithmetic that is accounting rather than forecast (gross public debt >100% of GDP by 2029, net interest 2%->3% of GDP, P95 Debt-at-Risk 117%). Firm 24/7 power plus the grid behind it is the most capital-intensive asset in the complex; a WACC held 150-200bp above the exogenous-demographics case mechanically truncates the buildout. AI-Q3's P50 is therefore too HIGH by my lens -- I would centre nearer 850-900 TWh -- and correspondingly AI-Q4 (66% impairment/revenue-shortfall) is too LOW, nearer 72-75%, since the same arithmetic is what converts announced capex into impaired capex. (2) AI-Q2 (firm adoption >=50%) is too LOW once aging is a demand pull rather than only a drag: a near-deterministic shrinkage of OECD working-age headcount with the old-age ratio going 31%->40% is the strongest adoption-forcing variable in the historical record of labour-saving technology (Japan robot density 1995-2015; US 1942-45 female participation; Black Death wage/mechanisation literature). Adoption of a cheap tool is a diffusion curve with a labour-cost denominator, and that denominator is locked. I would mark AI-Q2 up to ~28-30%. (3) AI-Q1 (TFP >= +0.50 pp/yr) is the one I would NOT move up despite (2), and this is the sharpest tension: Baumol/weakest-link composition means the same demographics that force adoption also shift the output share toward the non-automatable tasks whose shadow prices are rising (ISIC F and Q), so measured aggregate TFP is dragged by reweighting even while automatable-sector TFP accelerates. Endogenising demographics raises adoption and simultaneously lowers the aggregate TFP read-through from any given adoption level. The joint distribution implied by coupling therefore has a POSITIVE correlation between AI-Q2 and AI-Q4 (adopt hard, impair hard) and a NEGATIVE correlation between AI-Q2 and AI-Q1, neither of which is visible when 2B is scored marginal-by-marginal. Finally, AI-Q5 (cognitive labour share -3.5pp) is too low at 38.2%: the labour-scarcity wage signal from 2A is concentrated in exactly the sectors NOT in J/K/M, so the compensation-share decline in J/K/M is over-determined by the demographic composition shift even absent any AI displacement. I would mark it to ~44%. Note the honest counter-tension against my own CQ3: if AI-Q2 is really 28-30% and the healthy-aging +0.4 pp/yr offset in 2A is real, my CQ3 P50 of 1.9% may be ~15-20bp too low, and I have NOT adjusted for it, because my lens forbids me from pricing the capability trajectory that would convert adoption into output.
wave1.cq1_reasoning: Reference class 1 (conjunct A: OECD-38 harmonized unemployment 5-yr average <=5.5%). Verified from FRED OECD harmonised series this session: ~6.0-6.3% through 2000, peak ~8.4-8.5% early 2010, trough ~5.3-5.4% late 2019, ~4.9% through 2024 (FRED LRHUTTTTO1M156S discontinued series and OECDLRHUTTTTSTSAQ 15+ series; series differ in age coverage, and I could not retrieve a clean single annual harmonised series back to 1990, so the 1990s readings are approximate). Of roughly 30 rolling 5-year windows 1990-2026, only the window centred on 2022-2026 averages <=5.5%. Unconditional base rate ~3-8%. But the question window is 2032-2036 and the current level is 4.9%, i.e. 60bp of headroom, and the mechanical content of the locked prior is on my side: the OECD old-age ratio going ~31%->39-41% shrinks the working-age denominator near-deterministically, which is the Japan mechanism (Japan ran 2.4-3.0% unemployment through its own 40% old-age-ratio decade). The offsetting base rate is cyclical: historically a cyclical low in OECD unemployment persists 2-4 years, not 10, and a 5-year average 6-10 years out almost always contains at least one recession (base rate of >=1 OECD recession per 5-year window since 1960: ~60-70%), which adds 80-150bp to the window average. Net conjunct A = 45%. Reference class 2 (conjunct B: cumulative real median hourly wage growth in ISIC F+Q exceeding J+K+M by >=10.0 pp over 11 years). Mechanically that is only 0.87 pp/yr of differential sustained for 11 years, and differentials of that size are common -- US college/non-college diverged ~1 pp/yr for ~25 years (1979-2004). The rarity is entirely in the SIGN. Health/social care and construction have been the broad-sector laggards across the OECD for four decades; information, finance and professional services the leaders. Precedents for the required direction: US construction 2003-2007; the post-COVID low-wage compression 2019-2024 (Autor-Dube-McGrew measured roughly 5-8 pp of cumulative catch-up at the wage-percentile, not ISIC-sector, level). I find no OECD-wide 11-year window since 1970 in which F+Q beat J+K+M by >=10 pp at the broad-sector median. Base rate across (country x 11-year window) cases: ~10-20%. Conjunct B = 22%. Correlation: strongly positive and mechanistically the same story -- the labour scarcity that holds unemployment at 4.5-5.5% IS the wage signal that lifts F+Q, and a recession that breaks conjunct A also breaks conjunct B. rho = +0.35. Joint = 0.45*0.22 + 0.35*sqrt(0.45*0.55*0.22*0.78) = 0.099 + 0.35*0.2061 = 0.099 + 0.072 = 0.171. Adjustment: harmonized OECD-38 real MEDIAN HOURLY wage by ISIC letter grouping over 11 years is a measurement that does not currently exist cleanly for 38 countries; the base rate of hard-to-measure conjuncts resolving YES is below their modelled probability. Shade to 16.
wave1.cq2_reasoning: Conjunct A (GDP-weighted OECD-38 core CPI/PCE >=2.50%/yr average 2027-2036). Reference class: OECD core inflation decade averages -- 1970s ~9%, 1980s ~6%, 1990s ~3.5%, 2000s ~2.0%, 2010s ~1.6%, 2020-2025 ~3.3%. Four of six decades clear 2.5%, but the relevant reference class is the credible-inflation-targeting era: 1996-2005 ~2.1%, 2006-2015 ~1.8%, 2016-2025 ~2.6% (and that last one only clears because it contains the 2021-23 shock). One of three IT-era decades = 33%. Mechanical adjustments my lens permits: health and long-term care are ~9-12% of the advanced-economy CPI basket and their relative price rises arithmetically with the old-age ratio under Baumol (a composition identity, not a mechanism forecast); and the fiscal arithmetic in 2A -- gross debt >100% of GDP, net interest 2%->3% of GDP, China pension subsidies already ~10.1% of fiscal expenditure -- raises the historical frequency of inflation-target undershoot being tolerated rather than defended. Historical base rate of a sovereign with net interest >3% of GDP and a rising old-age ratio averaging under-target core inflation for a decade is low. Conjunct A = 44%. Conjunct B (China headline CPI <1.50%/yr average 2027-2036). Reference class: China CPI decade averages -- 1990s ~7.5%, 2000s ~1.8%, 2010s ~2.0%, 2020-2025 ~0.6% with 2023/2024/2025 at roughly 0.2%/0.2%/~0.0%. The dominant reference class is the Japan analogue: once an economy with a shrinking population and a deflating property stock enters a sub-1.5% CPI regime, it has stayed there for every subsequent decade on record (Japan 1995-2005 ~-0.1%, 2005-2015 ~0.2%, 2015-2025 ~1.0%). Base rate of exiting upward within 10 years: roughly 1 in 3 at best, and 2A's locked demographics (-60M population 2026-2035, worker/retiree 4.4->2.8) are the Japan configuration, only steeper. Conjunct B = 62%; the 38% complement is RMB devaluation pass-through, food/energy shocks, and a consumption-stimulus pivot. Correlation: mildly NEGATIVE, rho = -0.10. The two conjuncts describe a coherent bifurcated world (OECD services/care inflation with Chinese excess-capacity goods deflation), but the channel that delivers China's sub-1.5% print -- exported manufacturing deflation -- is also a direct suppressant of OECD core goods inflation, so the conjuncts fight each other slightly at the margin. Joint = 0.44*0.62 + (-0.10)*sqrt(0.44*0.56*0.62*0.38) = 0.273 - 0.10*0.2410 = 0.273 - 0.024 = 0.249. CQ2 = 25.
wave1.cq3_reasoning: Mandated reference class: 5-year windows of OECD+China PPP-weighted real growth since 1960. My reconstruction of the block (OECD-38 + China, PPP-weighted): 1960s ~5.0%, 1970s ~4.0%, 1980s ~4.0%, 1990s ~3.6%, 2000s ~3.2%, 2010-2019 ~3.2%, 2015-2019 ~3.4%, 2020-2024 ~2.6%. Mapped to the CQ6 bands, the unconditional distribution is brutal for my own answer: roughly 85-90% of all rolling 5-year windows since 1965 landed >=2.6% (band A territory), ~12-15% landed <2.0% (the 1979-83, 2008-12 and 2020-24 clusters), and essentially NONE landed below 1.5%. Pure outside view with no adjustment would give P50 ~3.0%. I depart from that by ~110bp, and the entire departure is arithmetic rather than mechanism, which is what my lens permits. Two pieces. (1) PPP weights. The block is ~64-65% of world PPP GDP; within it China is ~30% and OECD-38 ~70% today, drifting to roughly China 32% / OECD 68% by 2032-2036. China's contribution to the block's growth was 0.30*10.0 = 3.0 pp in the 2000s at a smaller weight; at a 32% weight and a 3.0% growth rate it contributes 0.96 pp. That single reweighting-plus-deceleration arithmetic removes ~1.5-2.0 pp from the block relative to every pre-2015 window in the reference class, and it is why the unconditional base rate is non-stationary here. The locked prior's -2.7 pp/yr China aging drag times a ~0.32 PPP weight is ~-0.86 pp on the block, the largest single term in the answer. (2) OECD arithmetic. The locked prior gives OECD baseline real GDP per capita at 0.6%/yr for 2036 (down from 1.0%) absent productivity offsets; OECD population growth is ~0.2-0.25%/yr and falling. Mechanical OECD GDP growth = ~0.85%/yr. I mark that UP to 1.2% because the historical base rate of a 5-year OECD window with zero productivity offset is low -- the lowest non-crisis OECD 5-year averages are ~1.3% -- and because 2A itself books a +0.4 pp/yr healthy-aging offset. Build-up: 0.68*1.2 + 0.32*3.0 = 0.82 + 0.96 = 1.78%. China's 3.0% is itself a reference-class number, not a forecast: post-catch-up decelerations at China's income level ran Japan 1991-1996 ~1.4%, Korea 2012-2019 ~2.9%, Taiwan 2000-2010 ~4.0%. Spread. OECD sigma ~0.66 (P10/P90 0.4/2.1), China sigma ~1.41 (P10/P90 1.0/4.6), weighted contributions 0.45 and 0.45, rho ~0.5 -> block sigma = sqrt(0.2025+0.2025+0.2025) = 0.78. Symmetric P10/P90 would be 0.81/2.81. I skew the distribution: the downside is fattened because the locked AI-Q4 marginal (66% impairment/revenue shortfall in 2027-2032) means a capex-bust recession is more likely than not somewhere in the run-up, and a 5-year window that contains the digestion phase prints 60-100bp below trend; the upside is fattened slightly less, by the healthy-aging offset and the possibility that the OECD 0.6% baseline is simply too pessimistic versus its own history. Final: P10 0.7 / P50 1.9 / P90 3.0. I flag explicitly that P10 = 0.7% has NO precedent in the reference class -- no 5-year window of this block since 1960 has printed below ~1.3% -- and I am assigning it 10% purely on the China-weight arithmetic.
wave1.cq4_reasoning: Mandated reference class: G7 10y real yield distribution by decade. Approximate GDP-weighted G7 10y real yields: 1970s ~-1.0% to 0% (ex-post negative; the inflation-surprise decade), 1980s ~+4.5%, 1990s ~+4.0%, 2000s ~+2.0%, 2010-2019 ~+0.3% (US ~0.6%, Bunds negative late, JGB real ~0), 2020-2024 ~+0.3% rising to ~+1.1-1.3% by 2024-25. Long-run 1960-2024 mean ~+2.0-2.5%. Starting point, built from the locked prior: US 10y TIPS 2.60% (FRED DFII10, Oct 30 2026) at a ~50% G7 GDP weight, with Japan ~0.6%, Germany ~1.4%, UK ~1.8%, France ~1.8%, Italy ~2.4%, Canada ~1.9% -> GDP-weighted start ~2.0%. Second mandated base rate: does a decade-average real yield stay near its starting level? No -- decade-over-decade changes in the G7 average have been large (-1 -> +4.5 -> +4.0 -> +2.0 -> +0.3 -> +1.1), mean absolute decade change ~1.5-2.0 pp. But at the 5-10 year horizon the level is highly persistent (estimated half-lives of real-rate deviations 5-15 years), so the best single predictor of the 2032-2036 average is the 2026 level, with wide error. Central: anchor at 2.0%, apply a small upward tilt. The tilt is arithmetic, not mechanism: 2A books gross public debt >100% of GDP by 2029 (~142% US, ~127% China by 2031), net interest 2%->3% of GDP, P95 Debt-at-Risk 117% of GDP, eroding sovereign convenience yields, and -- critically -- the IMF's own statement that aging worsens global (r-g) by ~+1.0 pp even where a frictionless r* eases. Supply arithmetic of that size has historically coincided with a higher term premium, not a lower one. P50 = 2.1%. Spread: sigma ~1.0-1.1 pp. P90 = 3.4%: the base rate of a 5-year G7 real-yield average >=3.4% is ~15-20% of post-1970 windows (the 1980s and early-1990s cluster), which from a 2.0% start is an upward move of 1.4 pp -- less than one historical decade-change. I keep it at the 10th-from-top percentile because getting there from 2.0% requires either a Volcker-style disinflation or a genuine term-premium repricing, not both. P10 = 0.8%: requires a return to the 2010s regime -- QE, a demand shortfall, a capex bust pushing r* down. That regime occupied the whole 2010-2021 period, i.e. a large share of recent windows, so 10% is if anything stingy; the reason I do not go higher is that the fiscal arithmetic is a one-way ratchet on supply and the 2010s regime also required a central-bank bid for duration that the locked debt path makes less likely to be redeployed at scale. Final: 0.8 / 2.1 / 3.4.
wave1.cq5_reasoning: Conjunct A (ICE BofA MOVE 10-year average >=105, 2027-2036). Mandated reference class: MOVE since 1988. CAVEAT, stated per the discipline rule -- I attempted to retrieve verified annual averages this session and could NOT; public search returned only per-year open/close/high/low (ConvexTrade, 2002-2026) and the 1988 start date, no annual means. The following are my own recollected annual averages and should be treated as unverified: late-1980s/1990s ~95-115; 1995-2004 ~95-105; 2008 ~175; 2000-2009 ~105; 2010-2019 ~75 (2017 ~52, 2019 ~65); 2020 ~70; 2021 ~62; 2022 ~122; 2023 ~122; 2024 ~95-100; 2025 ~75-85 (consistent with the retrieved 2025 open 96.67 / close 63.96 and 2023 open 129.97 / close 114.62). Of ~28 rolling 10-year windows (1988-1997 through 2016-2025), those averaging >=105 are roughly the earliest two and the 1999-2008/2000-2009 pair: 5-8 of 28, base rate ~20-28%. Mechanical adjustment: MOVE is a basis-point (not proportional) vol measure, so it is arithmetically higher when the level of rates is higher -- the >=105 windows are precisely the higher-rate-level windows, and the locked starting point is a 2.60% US real yield rather than the ~0% of 2012-2021. Conjunct A = 45%. Conjunct B (>=1 episode of MSCI World -25% peak-to-trough with G7 GDP-weighted 10y nominal failing to fall >=50bp, or rising >=25bp, in the drawdown window). Two nested base rates. (i) Frequency of a >=25% MSCI World drawdown inside a 10-year window: episodes since 1970 are 1973-74, 1980-82, 1987, ~1990, 2000-02, 2007-09, 2020, 2022. Almost every 10-year window contains one; the clear exceptions are 1991-1999 and 2010-2019 (2011 ~-22%, 2015-16 ~-19%, 2018 ~-18% all fell short). Base rate ~85-88%. (ii) CONDITIONAL on such a drawdown, frequency that bonds failed to rally: 1973-74 yields rose (YES), 1981-82 yields rose through most of the drawdown (YES), Aug-Oct 1987 yields rose ~150bp into the crash (YES, marginal), 1990 G7-weighted fell only ~40bp with JGB yields rising (ambiguous, score 0.5), 2000-02 US 10y 6.5%->3.6% (NO), 2007-09 sharp rally (NO), 2020 sharp rally (NO), 2022 yields rose ~200bp (YES). So ~3.5-4 of 8 = ~45%. That is the central historical fact for this question: the flight-to-quality bid is not a law, it is a low-inflation-regime property, and it failed in every inflation-driven or supply-driven drawdown. With ~1.4 expected qualifying drawdowns per 10-year window: P = 0.87 * [1-(1-0.45)^1.4] ~ 0.87*0.58 ~ 0.50; I mark to 48% for the ambiguity in the 1987 and 1990 codings. Correlation: strongly positive, rho = +0.45 -- a high-MOVE decade and a failed-flight-to-quality decade are the same regime (1970s-80s, 2022), and a low-MOVE decade mechanically produces the working flight-to-quality bid (2000-02, 2008, 2020). Joint = 0.45*0.48 + 0.45*sqrt(0.45*0.55*0.48*0.52) = 0.216 + 0.45*0.2486 = 0.216 + 0.112 = 0.328. CQ5 = 33. I note without pricing it that the locked ~$1.4T circular commitments / ~$650B debt issuance and the +2.4 pp Debt-at-Risk sensitivity to a 20% AI-led equity shock describe exactly the levered-basis-trade transmission channel that converts an equity drawdown into a Treasury selloff -- but that is a mechanism specific to this episode, so my lens forbids me from adjusting on it.
wave1.cq6_reasoning: Derived mechanically from my own CQ3 and CQ2 under the lexical-priority lock, not assigned freehand. Inputs: CQ3 = 0.7/1.9/3.0, implied sigma ~0.90 with a fattened lower tail. OECD-38 GDP-weighted core inflation over the 2032-2036 sub-window, derived from my CQ2 conjunct A (P(10-yr 2027-2036 core >=2.50%) = 44%) with sub-window variance widened: P(core >=2.7%) ~ 33%, P(core <2.0%) ~ 28%. Step 1, A: P(growth >=2.6%) = 1 - Phi((2.6-1.9)/0.90) = 1 - Phi(0.78) = 21.8%; I take 19 because my upper tail is thinner than normal (the OECD per-capita arithmetic caps it -- getting the block to 2.6% requires OECD GDP growth above 2.0%, which needs ~1.75%/yr OECD per-capita growth, a rate only the 1995-2004 US window delivered OECD-wide). A = 19. Step 2, C (second in lexical order): P(growth <2.0%) = Phi((2.0-1.9)/0.90) = Phi(0.11) = 54%; times P(core >=2.7%) = 33%. Independent product = 17.8%. I hold ~18 rather than adjusting: conditional on growth <2.0%, core >=2.7% is MORE likely if the cause is supply walls (grid, care, construction) and LESS likely if the cause is a demand/capex bust, and those two offset. C = 18. Step 3, D: P(growth <1.7%) = Phi((1.7-1.9)/0.90) = Phi(-0.22) = 41%; times P(core <2.0%) = 28% -> 11.5%. I mark UP to 14 because the locked AI-Q4 marginal (66%) makes a capex-digestion bust the single most likely route into growth <1.7%, and that route is positively correlated with core <2.0% (post-bust excess capacity, the BIS Box C labour-income demand deficit). D = 14. Step 4, B = residual = 100 - 19 - 18 - 14 = 49. Sum = 100 exactly. CONSISTENCY CHECK AGAINST MY OWN CQ3: my P50 is 1.9%, which sits inside B's literal 1.7-2.5% band, so B must be the modal regime -- it is, at 49. A at 19 is within 3 points of the direct normal-tail reading of my own CQ3 (21.8%), so I am not smuggling optimism into CQ6 that CQ3 denies. The combined low-growth mass C+D = 32 against my CQ3's P(growth <2.0%) = 54%: the 22-point gap is the leftover cell (growth <2.0% with core between 2.0% and 2.7%), which the lock explicitly routes to B -- so B's 49 decomposes as roughly 27 from the literal 1.7-2.5% band and 22 from that leftover cell. That reconciles. CONSISTENCY CHECK AGAINST MY OWN CQ2 (25): CQ2 needs core >=2.50% over the longer 2027-2036 window AND China <1.5%. My C regime needs the stricter core >=2.70% over the shorter 2032-2036 window AND growth <2.0%, so C (18) must be strictly smaller than the core-only term in CQ2 -- it is: 18 < P(core >=2.7% in 2032-36) = 33 < P(core >=2.5%) = 40, and 25 = 0.44*0.62 net of correlation sits between. No contradiction. OUTSIDE-VIEW DISCLOSURE: the unconditional historical base rate puts 85-90% of 5-year windows of this block in band A. My A = 19 is a 65-70 point departure from the raw base rate, and the whole departure rests on two arithmetic facts -- China's ~30-32% PPP weight multiplied by a decelerating growth rate, and the near-deterministic OECD old-age ratio path. If either of those is wrong, this distribution is wrong in one direction only: toward A.

hypothesis_critique.a: The failing word is "smoothly", and it fails on the most reliable base rate in labour economics: large-scale cross-occupational reallocation has never been smooth in any measured episode. US manufacturing displacement 1979-2010 -- Autor-Dorn-Hanson found local labour markets had not cleared a decade after the shock, with displaced workers exiting the labour force or claiming disability rather than relocating sectorally. UK coalfields 1984-2004: 20-year non-employment persistence. The secondary failure is in "supply the workers": elder care is credential-gated (licensing, clinical hours, background checks) and geographically non-tradable, while the white-collar savings are in metros, in different age cohorts, and in people with no clinical training -- the two populations barely intersect. Base rate of a predicted labour-reallocation offset arriving within a decade: near zero. A weaker version -- "AI frees enough fiscal room and enough hours that care staffing deteriorates less than it otherwise would" -- would score 45+. As stated, 5.
hypothesis_critique.b: Two words fail. "Blocks" overstates the mechanism: the plank conflates cross-border VIRTUAL services exports with PHYSICAL labour migration, and AI touches only the first. The demographic pull in 2A -- OECD old-age ratio 31%->40% -- is a near-deterministic bid for physically-present care and construction labour, which is where the Philippines' and India's migration channel actually sits; that channel gets STRONGER, not blocked. "Severely" fails on the base rate: Indian IT-BPO was forecast to be destroyed by the end of Y2K remediation (1999-2001), by the GFC (2008-09), and by RPA/automation (2015-2020), and revenue compounded through all three -- roughly $8B to $250B+ across those predicted extinctions. The historical pattern is margin and pricing-model compression, not revenue collapse, because each wave converted a labour-arbitrage business into an implementation-and-integration business. The defensible residual is that seat-based pricing erodes and the per-head value-add falls, which is damaging to the sector's equity multiple (reflected in my regime-D mark of -2.0%) and not at all the same as severe national suffering. 12.
hypothesis_critique.c: The failing word is "then" -- the plank's content is entirely in its timing claim, and timed inflation-turn forecasts have a poor base rate. Note the plank is also already partly stale on the locked priors: OECD core at ~2.5-2.8% US / ~2.2% euro area is not "hot" by any historical standard (the 1970s decade average was ~9%), so the first clause is near-vacuously true and does no work. The second clause -- falling in the 2030s -- runs directly against the arithmetic I can defend: health and long-term care are ~9-12% of the advanced-economy CPI basket and their relative price rises mechanically with the old-age ratio under Baumol, and the fiscal block (net interest 2%->3% of GDP, gross debt >100%) raises the historical frequency of tolerated overshoot. The plank is right in band D (14% of my mass) and in part of B, wrong in band C (18%). It also has a real base rate behind it: 1980s->1990s and 1990s->2000s both delivered exactly the decade-over-decade fall it describes, which is why this is the only plank I score near a coin-flip rather than dismissively. 33.
hypothesis_critique.d: Two words fail, and they fail in opposite directions. "Eventually" makes the plank unfalsifiable at the Dec 31, 2036 horizon -- an unbounded horizon converts a forecast into a tautology, and a claim that cannot resolve by the resolution date is not a claim. "Wins" is undefined and, on any natural reading (per-capita growth back to ~2%/yr, or coupled block growth >=2.6%), my CQ3 puts it at 19%. The governing base rate is the mandated one: forecasts that "technology will offset demography" resolving true at a dated horizon. Japan 1990-2025 ran the world's highest robot density against the world's steepest aging and delivered ~0.9%/yr GDP growth -- the offset claim was made repeatedly and resolved false each decade. The US 1995-2004 IT boom is the one genuine success, and it lasted nine years and did not persist. The 2010s automation-displacement forecasts produced a Solow-paradox redux instead. Base rate ~10-20%. The deeper structural objection is the one my effort brief names: under Chad Jones / Baumol weakest-link elasticities, automating a subset of complementary tasks raises the shadow price of the un-automated remainder, so "exponential" in one subset does not compound into aggregate output -- it compounds into relative-price shifts. Aggregate growth is capped by the slowest complementary task, and care and construction are the slow tasks. 15.

key_drivers: China's PPP weight inside the block (~30% now, ~32% by 2032-36) multiplied by its decelerating growth rate. This is the single largest term in CQ3 and the main reason I depart from the 85-90% historical base rate for growth >=2.6%: China contributed ~3.0 pp to block growth in the 2000s and contributes ~0.96 pp at 3.0% growth. The locked -2.7 pp/yr China aging drag times a 0.32 weight is ~-0.86 pp on the block, and is near-deterministic over ten years because the cohorts already exist.

The non-stationarity of the mandated reference class. Every base rate I was asked to anchor on (OECD+China growth windows, OECD unemployment averages, G7 real yields) is drawn from a period in which the block's demographic headcount was growing and China was converging. The arithmetic of 2A invalidates the unconditional frequency without giving me a replacement frequency, which is why my CQ3 and CQ6-A sit far from their raw base rates while my CQ4 and CQ5 sit close to theirs (real yields and vol regimes have no comparable mechanical break).

The conjunction discount on CQ1, CQ2 and CQ5. All three require two things, and in each case the historically rarer conjunct dominates: CQ1's sign-reversal in sector wage leadership (22%), CQ2's OECD core >=2.50% for a decade in the inflation-targeting era (44%), CQ5's failed flight-to-quality (48%). Correlations are +0.35, -0.10 and +0.45 respectively, and the sign of the correlation moves the joint by 7, -2 and +11 points -- i.e. the correlation assumption matters as much as the marginals for CQ5.

The level of rates as a mechanical driver of measured volatility and of asset spreads. MOVE is a basis-point measure, so a 2.0-2.1% G7 real yield regime arithmetically supports a higher index than the ~0% regime of 2012-2021; this is what takes CQ5 conjunct A from a ~25% raw base rate to 45%, and it is also what drives the C-vs-D spread across every duration-sensitive asset in the matrix.

The capex-supercycle impairment base rate (rail 1870s, telecom/fibre 1999-2002, shale 2014-2020, nuclear 1980s, Japan 1980s): announced capex was >=20% impaired in roughly 70-80% of historical cases, and in every case the owners of the resulting operating assets (power, grid, right-of-way) fared far better than the capital-raisers. This is the organising principle of the asset matrix -- it is why the power/grid chain carries the highest buildout number (8.0%) while the AI complex carries 1.0%, and why the AI complex is the most regime-dispersed asset (9.0% in A to -6.0% in D).

The historical frequency of correlated equity-bond drawdowns being a regime property, not a constant: bonds failed to rally in 1973-74, 1981-82, 1987 and 2022 (inflation- or vol-driven shocks) and rallied hard in 2000-02, 2007-09 and 2020 (disinflationary shocks). At ~45% conditional frequency this is close to a coin flip, which is why the single largest cross-regime spread in my matrix is G7 long nominal bonds at -4.5% in C versus +5.5% in D.
wave1.lens_self_description: I answered purely as an outside-view base-rate scout: for each question I located the widest defensible historical reference class, read its frequency, and adjusted only for the mechanical arithmetic in the locked priors (demographic headcount, PPP weights, debt accounting, the basis-point construction of MOVE) -- which forbade me from reasoning about AI capability trajectories, model releases, scaling behaviour, diffusion mechanics, or any mechanism specific to this episode, and forced me to disclose every point where I departed from the raw base rate and by how much.

AI/hyperscaler complex (mega-cap tech + semis + AI infra)

wave1.coupling_tension: THREE inconsistencies, with directions. (1) PRIMARY, downward: AI-Q1 (23.0% for TFP >= +0.50 pp/yr) is too HIGH once demographics are endogenous. 2B treats the sectoral composition of value added as fixed. It is not: aging is a forced reallocation of expenditure toward the zero-productivity-growth bundle. The care+construction+grid share of OECD GVA rises from ~19% to ~23% by 2036 purely from 65+ headcount (+3%/yr) and the electrification/datacenter build. Measured aggregate TFP is the share-weighted sum, so even with the AI-exposed slice's within-sector TFP unchanged at +2.5%/yr, the reweighting subtracts ~0.12 pp/yr by 2032-36, and the Hulten/Aghion-Jones price effect subtracts more (the automated slice's nominal share falls as its relative price falls). Endogenizing demographics should move AI-Q1 from 23.0% to ~17-18%. Note this is a measurement-and-weights argument, not a claim that the technology is weaker: AI-Q2-style adoption can be higher at the same time as AI-Q1 is lower. (2) Upward: AI-Q2 (21.3% for >=50% of firms >=10 employees) is too LOW. The adoption decision is driven by the wage-to-automation-cost ratio, and aging raises the numerator exogenously in exactly the small-firm, non-tradable, labour-scarce segment that is the denominator of AI-Q2. With adoption elasticity +0.5 to that ratio and real labour cost in scarce occupations rising 15-25% by 2036, AI-Q2 should rise several points, to ~25-27%. The coupled joint distribution therefore has POSITIVE adoption and WEAKER measured aggregate TFP simultaneously — a combination that 2B's exogenous-demographics framing treats as near-contradictory and that the Jagged-Diffusion regime only half captures. (3) Upper-tail compression: AI-Q3's P90 of 1,573.8 TWh is too high because the binding input on datacenter load is not chips, capital or even generation but licensed high-voltage electricians, linemen and interconnection throughput — the same shrinking skilled-trades pool that grid hardening, housing and care-facility construction bid for. Endogenous demographics shrink that pool. I would cut the P90 to ~1,350 TWh while leaving P50 roughly intact, because the constraint binds on the tail, not the median.
wave1.cq1_reasoning: Conjunct 1 (OECD-38 harmonized unemployment <= 5.5% average over 2032-36): marginal 60%. Mechanism, not base rate: the denominator is shrinking. OECD 20-64 population falls ~0.3%/yr by the early 2030s while the 65+/20-64 ratio goes 31% -> 39-41% (2A, observed). A shrinking labour force mechanically suppresses the equilibrium unemployment rate at any given level of labour demand — this is a quantity-side arrow, and it is the strongest single force on this conjunct. Against it: AI-Q4 at 66% (observed) places a capex impairment/revenue-shortfall episode in 2027-2032, and the digestion tail plausibly runs into 2032-33 with elevated cognitive-sector separations; a 5-year AVERAGE above 5.5% requires roughly two years near 6.5%, which only a genuine BIS-style demand shortfall (my regime D, 17%) delivers. 60% it is. Conjunct 2 (F+Q real median hourly wage beats J+K+M by >= 10.0 pp cumulative 2025-2036, i.e. ~0.87 pp/yr differential for 11 years): marginal 22%. This is where my mechanism says the intuitive answer is wrong. Construction (F) is market-priced and will deliver: skilled-trades real wages +2.5 to +4.0%/yr on interconnection, grid and reshoring backlogs, i.e. +30-50% cumulative. But Q (health/social care) is ~70-80% publicly funded or administered-price in the OECD, and 2A gives the fiscal constraint as observed fact (net interest 2% -> 3% of GDP; China's 2.9T RMB pension subsidy as the analogue). Under fiscal monopsony the excess demand for care hours clears in QUANTITY, not price: unmet-need hours, waiting lists, higher client-to-aide ratios, informal family substitution. My wage-curve semi-elasticity is +0.30 for market-priced sectors and ~+0.08 for administered-price care — a monopsony wedge of ~0.25x. Q is roughly 60% of F+Q employment, so the composite F+Q real median wage gain is ~+1.2%/yr, not +3%. Meanwhile the J+K+M MEDIAN is not the J+K+M compensation SHARE (AI-Q5, 38.2%): if AI removes entry-level and junior cognitive roles first, the surviving distribution's MEDIAN rises by composition even as the sectoral wage bill share falls. That composition effect is a direct arithmetic obstacle to the 10 pp gap and is, in my view, the specific reason this conjunct fails. 22%. Correlation: both conjuncts are children of the same labour-scarcity node, so rho = +0.25. Joint = 0.60 x 0.22 + 0.25 x sqrt(0.24 x 0.1716) = 0.132 + 0.051 = 0.183 -> 18.

Joint = 0.52 x 0.62 - 0.15 x sqrt(0.2496 x 0.2356) = 0.322 - 0.036 = 0.286 -> 29. The OECD-38 dissaving transition is also only partly underway by 2032-36 (the big 55-64 saver cohort is still saving into ~2030): -20 bp. wave1.cq5_reasoning: Conjunct 1 (MOVE average >= 105 over 2027-2036): marginal 45%. Mechanism, no base rate: MOVE is a price of rate-uncertainty insurance, and its structural floor is set by (i) duration supply per unit of risk-bearing capacity and (ii) who holds the marginal Treasury. Both are observed to be deteriorating — debt past 100% of GDP, net interest to 3%, and levered hedge-fund basis-trade absorption replacing price-insensitive official and bank demand. Levered intermediation makes the vol process jumpy: each deleveraging episode spikes MOVE to 140-160, and the quiet-year floor rises from ~65 (the 2010s, when a central bank was the marginal buyer) to ~85-95. A 10-year average of >= 105 therefore needs roughly three stress years out of ten given a ~90 floor. That is close to a coin flip and slightly under: 45%. Conjunct 2 (one episode with MSCI World -25% peak-to-trough while G7 10y nominal fails to fall >= 50 bp, or rises >= 25 bp): marginal 26%, built as two terms. P(MSCI World >= -25% drawdown at some point in 2027-2036) = 70%, derived mechanically rather than frequentially: the AI complex is plausibly ~33-38% of MSCI World capitalization by 2029-2030, and AI-Q4 (observed, 66%) is essentially the condition for that complex to de-rate 40-50%, which alone contributes 14-18 pp of index drawdown before any multiplier through private credit, the $650B debt stack and the wealth-effect channel. Then P(the flight-to-quality bid FAILS | that drawdown) = 37%. The bid fails only in three identifiable states: an inflation/supply-driven shock (the correlation mechanism: when the inflation-innovation share of macro-shock variance exceeds roughly 50%, stock-bond correlation flips from about -0.3 to +0.4); a sovereign-credibility shock where the Treasury IS the source; or forced cross-asset deleveraging where the basis trade unwinds and dealers sell duration into the equity decline. Crucially, the MODAL path for an AI-capex bust is DISINFLATIONARY, so bonds rally and conjunct 2 fails — this is the key mechanical reason I am well below where intuition puts this question. 0.70 x 0.37 = 0.26. Correlation: high and positive, rho = +0.55, because the levered-intermediation mechanism that lifts average MOVE is the same one that breaks the correlation regime. Joint = 0.45 x 0.26 + 0.55 x sqrt(0.2475 x 0.1924) = 0.117 + 0.120 = 0.237 -> 22.

hypothesis_critique.a: The failure word is "smoothly", and a second failure hides in "supply". The mechanism has no transmission channel from a displaced 45-year-old insurance underwriter to a licensed care hour: the transition is occupational (zero skill overlap), geographic (cognitive jobs are metro-concentrated, care demand is where the old live), licensure-gated (RN/LPN/aide credentialing is a 1-4 year pipeline with a hard clinical-placement constraint), and wage-asymmetric (care median pays roughly 60-70% of the cognitive-services median, so the displaced worker's reservation wage exceeds the care offer and they exit the labour force or take a lower-skill adjacent job instead). Worse, the plank has the SIGN of the fiscal arrow wrong: AI-driven white-collar displacement SHRINKS the income-tax base that funds care, so the moment the labour is notionally available, the money to hire it is scarcer. "Supply" presumes a market clearing in wages; my mechanism clears it in rationing.
hypothesis_critique.b: Two failure words, "blocks" and "severely", and the plank fails because it collapses two channels the scope locks explicitly separate. VIRTUAL services exports are genuinely exposed, but at the bottom of the stack: L1 support, voice, transactional BPO, basic coding and transcription — call it 25-35% of the Philippines' ~1.7M BPO headcount and a smaller share of India's IT-services revenue, which is already migrating to AI-delivery, integration and managed-service margin capture (the implementation labour AI diffusion requires is itself an export). PHYSICAL labour migration moves in the OPPOSITE direction: the OECD 65+/20-64 ratio going to 39-41% is the largest care-migration PULL in modern history, and Philippine nursing and caregiver deployment plus Indian construction and health migration expand. AI does not block that channel at all — it cannot automate a bed bath. So the correct read is CHANNEL REALLOCATION with a terms-of-trade loss at the low-value-added end, not severe aggregate suffering. The one place I grant the plank force: remittance per worker from care migration is lower than BPO revenue per worker, so the composition shift is real even if the level is not catastrophic.
hypothesis_critique.c: The failure is the word "then" — the implied SEQUENCING, which my mechanism reverses. The near-term window (2027-2030) carries the strongest disinflationary forces in the whole horizon: compute and inference prices falling on a learning curve, AI-driven goods and tradable-services deflation, Chinese excess capacity exported into OECD goods prices, and above all the post-capex air pocket that AI-Q4 (66%, observed) places in 2028-2032. The 2030s are when the inflationary arrows actually bite: the care/construction/skilled-trades shadow prices peak, the 65+/20-64 ratio is through 40% and heading to 52%, net interest is at 3% of GDP so fiscal dominance is a live policy constraint, and grid supply walls are priced. So the shape is more like dip-then-grind-up, or a flat 2.3-2.7% plateau, than hot-then-cold. The plank's level claim for 2027-28 is defensible; its turning point is pointed the wrong way.
hypothesis_critique.d: Two failure words: "eventually" and "wins". "Eventually" smuggles in a horizon outside the resolution date — it is unfalsifiable at Dec 31 2036 and therefore not a forecast. "Wins" is the substantive error and it is an arithmetic one, not an attitude: with gross-complement task aggregation (my sigma = 0.4), aggregate growth is pulled toward the slowest-growing input AS THAT INPUT'S SHARE RISES, and the automated slice's nominal share FALLS precisely because its relative price falls (the Hulten / Aghion-Jones "Baumol's disease of growth" result). Exponential progress in a subset of tasks therefore yields a BOUNDED aggregate contribution — in my decomposition ~0.3-0.4 pp/yr net of reweighting — against a demographic drag that is large, monotone and arithmetically certain (China -2.7 pp/yr on a 0.36 PPP weight is -0.97 pp of the block before anything else happens). The plank is not wrong that AI's within-sector growth can be exponential; it is wrong that an exponential in a shrinking-share subsystem shows up as an exponential in the measured aggregate by 2036.

key_drivers: Baumol/Jones share reweighting: aging and electrification push the zero-productivity-growth bundle (care + construction + grid) from ~19% to ~23% of OECD GVA by 2036, which with substitution elasticity sigma = 0.4 mechanically subtracts ~0.12 pp/yr from measured aggregate TFP and sets the hard cap on CQ3 and on CQ6-A's 13%.

China's PPP weight of 0.36 within the OECD-38 + China block multiplied by its observed -2.7 pp/yr aging drag: roughly -0.97 pp of block growth, the single largest arithmetic term in the CQ3 answer and the reason the coupled number sits near 1.9% rather than near OECD-only intuitions.

WEAKEST LINK: licensed, physically-present human hours in regulated settings — high-voltage electricians, linemen and interconnection throughput on the grid/datacenter chain, and licensed nurses and care aides on the demographic chain. Substitution elasticity against AI capital ~0.2. By 2036 the electrical-trades shadow price shows up as +35-50% cumulative real wages and 4-7 year queues; the care shadow price rises ~+40% but the PAID price rises only ~+12-15% real, with the wedge appearing as rationed hours.

Fiscal monopsony in care: ~70-80% of OECD care is publicly funded, so the scarcity rent clears in quantity not price (wage semi-elasticity +0.08 administered vs +0.30 market-priced). This is why CQ1 is 18 despite the scarcity being completely real, and it is the mechanism that most distinguishes my answer from an intuitive one.

Debt supply plus eroding sovereign convenience yield: +2.5 bp of real 10y per +1 pp of public debt/GDP, applied to ~+18 pp of G7 debt/GDP, gives ~+45 bp and is the near-certain monotone arrow that makes CQ4's distribution right-skewed (P90 3.30 against P10 1.00).

Correlation-regime mechanism: when the inflation-innovation share of macro-shock variance crosses roughly 50%, stock-bond correlation flips from about -0.3 to +0.4. Levered basis-trade absorption of Treasury supply raises the MOVE floor from ~65 to ~90 and makes the vol process jumpy. But the modal AI-capex bust is DISINFLATIONARY, so bonds rally and CQ5's second conjunct fails in the most likely bad state — which is why CQ5 is 22 and not 45.
wave1.lens_self_description: I applied the Inside-View Causal-Mechanism Modeler lens: every number here is derived from an explicit transmission chain with signed arrows and written-down elasticities (task-bundle sigma = 0.4, Baumol reweighting -0.12 pp/yr, adoption elasticity +0.5 to the wage/automation-cost ratio, +2.5 bp real yield per pp of debt/GDP, +30 bp of r* per 1% of GDP of investment demand, wage semi-elasticity +0.30 market-priced versus +0.08 administered care), and the lens forbade me from using base rates, historical frequencies, reference-class analogies or any outside-view anchor — so where the mechanism and the historical frequency disagree (notably CQ1's wage-gap conjunct, CQ5's correlation break, and the hot-then-cold inflation path) I let the mechanism decide.

wave1.coupling_tension: Two 2B marginals stop being internally consistent once demographics are endogenous, and in my lens both fail through a MEASUREMENT/accounting channel rather than a behavioural one. (1) AI-Q1 (TFP >= +0.50 pp, 23.0%) is too HIGH conditional on AI-Q3's own P50 of ~998 TWh. Going 365 -> ~1,000 TWh by 2036 is ~+633 TWh, i.e. roughly +120 GW of average load, ~180-200 GW of nameplate IT load and ~350-500 GW of generation plus firming, which is ~$1.8-2.8T of generation and T&D capex drawn from exactly the ISIC F trade pool that demographic shrinkage is already thinning (OECD-38 construction workforce is older than the mean and loses ~1.5-2%/yr of hours to retirement over 2026-2036). Under Jones/Baumol weakest-link elasticities the shadow price of interconnection, transformer and licensed-electrician hours rises, and the TFP numerator is eaten by the complement. Standalone, exogenous-demographics elicitation cannot impose that AI-Q3-high must make AI-Q1-low; coupled, it must. I would mark AI-Q1 down to ~18-19% conditional on AI-Q3 P50 >= 950 TWh. Direction: DOWN. (2) AI-Q5 (J/K/M labour compensation share of sectoral GVA falls >= 3.5 pp, 38.2%) is too LOW, for accounting rather than labour-market reasons: the GVA denominator in J, K and M is inflated by SNA-2008 capitalization of software, data and R&D and by hyperscaler rent booking inside sector J, while demographic shrinkage of entering cohorts plus AI truncation of entry-level roles cuts the compensation numerator's headcount. Both move the ratio down mechanically, independent of any wage story. I would mark AI-Q5 up to ~48-52%. Direction: UP. The sharp conflict: AI-Q5 UP and AI-Q1 DOWN cannot both be read as "AI is working" - they are the same jagged-rent world, which is why my CQ6 mass concentrates in residual B rather than A.
wave1.cq2_reasoning:
RESOLVING SERIES. Conjunct 1: no official "GDP-weighted OECD-38 core CPI/PCE" exists. The nearest published object is OECD's CPI excluding food and energy for the OECD total, aggregated with household-final-consumption PPP weights, NOT GDP weights, and it includes ALL 38 members. The "/PCE" option lets US core PCE substitute for US core CPI; core PCE has run ~0.2-0.4 pp below core CPI structurally (rent weight, chain vs Laspeyres, medical pricing source), and the US is ~52% of any PPP-GDP-weighted OECD-38 aggregate - so the CPI/PCE fork alone is worth ~0.1-0.2 pp on the aggregate and ~5 pp on the probability, toward NO.
THE DOMINANT ARTEFACT (toward YES). GDP weighting OECD-38 at PPP puts Turkey at ~3.5-4%, Mexico ~3.5%, Poland ~2%, Colombia/Chile/Costa Rica/Hungary ~2.5% combined. Turkey alone, at even a 15%/yr average core print over 2027-2036 (it has not been below 8% in a decade), contributes ~+0.55 pp to the aggregate; at 25% it contributes ~+0.95 pp. The OECD aggregate CPI ran roughly double its ex-Turkey counterpart through 2022-2024 for this reason. A Germany/US/Japan-weighted mental model says ~2.1-2.3%; the literal OECD-38 GDP-weighted construction says ~3.0-3.4%. This single index-construction fact moves conjunct 1 from ~0.45 to ~0.88.
CONJUNCT 1 MARGINAL: construction-weighted. P(resolver uses the literal all-38 aggregate) 0.70, under which P = 0.88 -> 0.616. P(resolver silently uses an advanced-economy / G7-ish / ex-high-inflation construction) 0.30, under which P = 0.45 -> 0.135. Total 0.751 -> 0.75.
CONJUNCT 2: China headline CPI < 1.50%/yr average 2027-2036, NBS monthly CPI. Observed base: China headline CPI averaged well under 1% across 2023-2026, with outright negative prints. Structural supports for low prints are also MEASUREMENT facts: the NBS basket treats owner-occupied housing through a thin rental imputation (so the property cycle barely enters CPI), the basket is reweighted every five years with weight-shift effects that have historically damped the index, and food (pork cycle) is the main upside tail. Endogenous demographics reinforce: -60M population over 2026-2035, worker/retiree 4.4 -> 2.8, precautionary saving, excess manufacturing capacity exported as disinflation. A 10-year mean is forgiving - one 4% food-shock year adds only 0.25 pp to the mean. Risks to YES: a decisive reflation/fiscal-transfer pivot, RMB depreciation import channel, or a basket revision that adds services/housing. MARGINAL 0.72.
CORRELATION. Slightly NEGATIVE, and the channel is explicit: Chinese deflation is exported into OECD goods core, so the very force that satisfies conjunct 2 shaves OECD core. Offsetting positive channel: both are symptoms of the same bifurcated regime. Net factor ~0.95. JOINT = 0.75 x 0.72 x 0.95 = 0.513 -> 50.
This is deliberately far above a naive conjunction read, and the gap is almost entirely index construction, not macroeconomics - which is precisely my lens's claim.
wave1.cq3_reasoning:
RESOLVING SERIES AND ACCOUNTING. Resolution requires summing OECD National Accounts (SNA 2008) real GDP for 38 members plus NBS China real GDP, weighted by FIXED 2025 PPP shares (constant 2025 USD PPP, per the lock). Three accounting facts matter more than any forecast: (i) FIXED 2025 weights, not chain weights - China's PPP share of (OECD-38 + China) is ~35% (China ~$42T PPP vs OECD-38 ~$77T PPP in 2025) and is frozen there, so China's faster growth is never allowed to raise its own weight; chain-weighting would add ~+0.05-0.08 pp over five years. (ii) China's contribution is the single largest term: the locked IMF -2.7 pp/yr China aging drag times the 0.35 PPP weight is -0.95 pp on this aggregate - essentially the entire locked global -1.1 pp figure arrives through China at coupled weights. (iii) NBS real GDP has a documented upward bias from deflator construction and output smoothing (Nakamura-Steinsson-Liu and successor work put it at roughly 1-1.5 pp in boom years, less in slow years); resolution will use the official print, so the MEASURED coupled number sits ~+0.25-0.40 pp above the truth. I forecast the measured number, as instructed.
FERMI. OECD-38: locked baseline per-capita 0.6%/yr (down from 1.0% on the 31% -> 39-41% old-age ratio) plus OECD-38 population growth of ~0.20-0.30%/yr (migration-driven; US/Canada/Australia positive, Japan/Korea/Italy negative) = 0.80-0.90% aggregate. AI offset: with AI-Q1 at only 23% (and my coupled mark-down to ~19%) for >= +0.50 pp, expected TFP lift over 2032-36 is ~+0.25 pp, partly capitalized rather than productive. OECD-38 central 1.10-1.15%.
China: official ~4% targets decaying; IMF-type paths reach ~3% by 2030. Aging -2.7 pp, property deleveraging, 2.9T RMB pension subsidy (10.1% of fiscal expenditure) crowding capex. Central 2.85-2.95% on the OFFICIAL print.
COUPLED CENTRAL: 0.65 x 1.13 + 0.35 x 2.90 = 0.73 + 1.02 = 1.75%. Add +0.10 pp of pure measurement support (see below) -> P50 1.85%.
MEASUREMENT SUPPORT, UPWARD, ~+0.10 pp: the AI capex hump adds to measured GFCF and hence GDP during the buildout; critically, when the locked 66%-probability impairment event lands, a write-down is a BALANCE-SHEET revaluation, not negative GDP - measured output never gives the capex back. Hedonic/quality adjustment of GPU and software prices also converts nominal capex into large real volumes. Both inflate measured growth relative to welfare.
BAUMOL / JONES WEAKEST-LINK CAP. Where the cap binds by 2036: interconnection queues, HV transformer and switchgear lead times, licensed electrician and lineworker hours, and licensed care hours. With AI-Q3 P50 ~998 TWh requiring ~350-500 GW of generation plus firming, the non-automated complement's shadow price rises enough that even a Transformative Breakout TFP number does not pass through to aggregate output before 2036 - the physical queue is the binding constraint, and queue clearance is a 5-9 year process on observed 2024-2026 interconnection data. This is why my P90 is 2.65 rather than 3.2.
TAILS. P10 1.10: AI capex bust plus China property/local-government fiscal event plus one OECD recession year in the window (two of five years near zero). P90 2.65: genuine broad diffusion, China holding 4% official, OECD-38 at 1.7%. Right tail is capped by the weakest-link argument; left tail is cushioned by the NBS floor behaviour (China official prints have never gone below ~2.2% ex-2020 even in stress).
wave1.cq4_reasoning:
RESOLVING SERIES AND THE TWO FORKS THAT MOVE THE ANSWER MORE THAN MACRO DOES. Construction: 10y nominal benchmark minus 10y inflation swap OR TIPS breakeven, for each of 7 countries, GDP-weighted, averaged over 60 months. FORK 1 - swap vs breakeven: because breakeven is DEFINED as nominal minus the linker yield, "nominal minus TIPS breakeven" just returns the TIPS real yield, inclusive of the TIPS liquidity premium (+10-25 bp vs the true ex-ante real rate). "Nominal minus inflation swap" returns something else entirely: USD 10y zero-coupon inflation swaps have run ~15-30 bp ABOVE CPI breakevens (swap vs cash basis, CPI floor and indexation-lag conventions), so the swap route yields a real rate ~15-30 bp LOWER. The question's "/" is therefore a ~20-40 bp fork on the P50 - larger than most plausible macro disagreement about the 2032-36 path. FORK 2 - weighting: "GDP-weighted" is unspecified while the lock says PPP. At PPP, G7 weights are approximately US 0.523, Japan 0.113, Germany 0.105, UK 0.075, France 0.075, Italy 0.062, Canada 0.046; at market exchange rates the US rises to ~0.57 and Japan falls to ~0.07, which lifts the aggregate by ~+0.15 pp because Japan is the low outlier. COVERAGE GAPS: Italy and Canada have thin 10y inflation-swap markets and no deep linker curve (BTP Italia is CPI-FOI-linked and short); Japan's 10y JPY inflation swap is barely transactable and the JGBi curve is sparse. For at least 3 of 7 countries the stated construction is not cleanly computable, so resolution will interpolate or substitute survey breakevens - a further ~15 bp of construction noise. Also: if any G7 central bank reinstitutes yield-curve control or explicit caps (the "financial repression" leg of CQ6-C/D), the nominal benchmark stops being a market price and the computed real yield becomes an administered number - a definitional break, not an observation.
LEVELS. Anchor: US 10y TIPS real 2.60% (locked, FRED DFII10, 30 Oct 2026). For 2032-36 I take US 10y real averaging ~2.30%: upward pressure from gross public debt >100% of GDP (US ~142% by 2031), net interest 2% -> 3% of GDP, eroding sovereign convenience yields, levered basis-trade absorption of duration, retiree DISSAVING, and AI capital demand; downward pressure from the aging saving glut, a lower frictionless r*, and post-bust demand deficit. The locked IMF framing - (r - g) worsens by ~+1.0 pp even where r* eases - is exactly the "g collapses faster than r" shape, which keeps real yields high in level terms without requiring an r* surge.
Country reals used (2032-36 averages): US 2.30, Japan 0.50, Germany 1.10, UK 1.80, France 1.80, Italy 2.60, Canada 1.80. PPP-weighted = 1.203 + 0.057 + 0.116 + 0.135 + 0.135 + 0.161 + 0.083 = 1.89%. Round P50 to 1.95 to split the swap/breakeven and PPP/market-rate forks.
TAILS, RIGHT-SKEWED. P10 0.90: CQ6-D demand shortfall plus explicit repression - QE/YCC return, breakevens hold up while nominals are capped, Japanification of Germany and Canada. P90 3.15: CQ6-C fiscal dominance with a term-premium spike; Debt-at-Risk P95 at 117% of GDP (+2.4 pp on a 20% AI-led equity shock) is the stated tail, and a sustained 5-year AVERAGE above 3% requires that tail to persist rather than spike, which is why P90 is 3.15 and not 4.0.
wave1.cq5_reasoning:
RESOLVING SERIES. Conjunct 1: ICE BofA MOVE Index (MOVE), a 1-month option-implied NORMALIZED BASIS-POINT yield-volatility index, weighted 20/20/40/20 across the 2y/5y/10y/30y CMT tenors. The decisive construction fact: MOVE is a bp-vol index, so its level scales roughly with the LEVEL of yields. Historical averages: ~100-110 (2000-2010, high-yield era), ~70 (2011-2019, ZIRP era), ~60 (2019 and 2021), ~110-125 (2023-2024), ~80-95 (2025-2026). A 10-year MEAN >= 105 therefore effectively requires both sustained high nominal yields AND repeated vol episodes; mean reversion in realized vol between episodes is the enemy of the threshold. Index risk: ICE has restructured MOVE's construction before (the move from the legacy Merrill specification to the current CMT-based weighting); over a 10-year window there is a ~12-15% chance of a methodology change, licensing change or discontinuation, direction unknown but it creates a void/ambiguity branch. MARGINAL conjunct 1: 0.42.
Conjunct 2: (a) MSCI World (which index version - price, net, gross, USD or local? peak-to-trough on DAILY closes vs month-end is worth several pp on a -25% threshold; daily closes make -25% materially easier) falls >= 25% peak-to-trough; (b) during that drawdown WINDOW, G7 GDP-weighted 10y nominal yields fail to fall >= 50 bp, or rise >= 25 bp.
(a) base rate: MSCI World had >= 25% USD drawdowns in 2000-02, 2007-09, 2020 (-34%) and 2022 (-26% intraday/close basis). Four in 26 years, with concentration now at a record and ~$1.4T of circular AI vendor/cloud/chip commitments backed by only ~$300B equity and ~$650B debt. Over 10 years: 0.70.
(b) conditional on (a), probability the drawdown is of the CORRELATED type rather than a flight-to-quality growth scare: 2022 is the template (yields rose hard into a -26% drawdown); the correlated type arises when the trigger is inflation, fiscal/term-premium, or a basis-trade/collateral deleveraging rather than a demand shock. Given fiscal dominance risk and levered hedge-fund basis-trade absorption of Treasury supply, I put the correlated share at ~0.45, raised to ~0.50 by two measurement artefacts: (i) "during the equity drawdown window" is a generous, resolver-chosen interval - peak date to trough date can be months, so "fail to fall by 50 bp" has many ways to be satisfied; (ii) the G7 GDP-WEIGHTED aggregate includes Japan at ~11% PPP weight with a structurally pinned/low-beta JGB 10y, which DAMPENS the aggregate's rally magnitude and makes "fail to fall by 50 bp" easier - worth ~+4-6 pp on its own, toward YES. Multiple independent drawdown draws over 10 years add a further uplift. Conjunct 2 = 0.70 x 0.50 x 1.09 (multi-draw) = 0.38.
CORRELATION: strongly positive. A world of repeated correlated equity-bond selloffs is mechanically a high-MOVE world, and a basis-trade deleveraging event IS a MOVE spike. P(conj1 | conj2) ~ 0.70 vs 0.42 unconditional. JOINT = 0.38 x 0.70 = 0.266; cross-check 0.42 x P(conj2|conj1)=0.62 = 0.260. Take 26.
Flagged >3 pp artefacts: Japan's pinned JGB inside the G7 nominal aggregate (+5 pp, toward YES); daily-close vs month-end peak-to-trough convention (+4 pp, toward YES); MOVE's bp-vol level dependence combined with any return to low nominal yields in regime D (-6 pp, toward NO); MOVE methodology-change/void branch (-3 pp, ambiguous).
wave1.cq6_reasoning:
LOCK CONFIRMED AND AUDITED. I apply the stated lexical priority exactly: (1) A if coupled growth >= 2.6; (2) else C if OECD-38 GDP-weighted core >= 2.7 AND growth < 2.0; (3) else D if growth < 1.7 AND core < 2.0; (4) else B. The rule is well-formed and exhaustive: step 1 partitions on growth alone, steps 2 and 3 are disjoint on core (>= 2.7 vs < 2.0), and step 4 absorbs everything else. Confirmed MECE under the lock.
CRITICAL: the CQ6 inflation measure is the SAME "GDP-weighted OECD-38 core" object audited in CQ2, so the Turkey/Mexico/Poland PPP-GDP-weight artefact (Turkey ~3.5-4% weight at even 15% core contributes ~+0.55 pp to the aggregate) applies here too. This is the single biggest driver of my CQ6 shape and it pushes mass from D into C and B.
STEP 1 - A. From my CQ3 (P10 1.10 / P50 1.85 / P90 2.65), P(growth >= 2.6) ~ 0.11. A = 11. Consistency check stated explicitly: my CQ3 P50 is 1.85%, so I cannot and do not put most mass on A; A sits just under my P90 exceedance.
STEP 2 - C. P(core >= 2.7 over 2032-36) = 0.70 x 0.60 (literal all-38 construction) + 0.30 x 0.22 (ex-high-inflation construction) = 0.486. P(growth < 2.0) = 0.60 from my CQ3 distribution. Mild positive dependence in a bottleneck world, factor 1.05: P(C) = 0.486 x 0.60 x 1.05 = 0.306, trimmed to 0.28 for the chance that a resolver who already chose an ex-Turkey construction in CQ2 applies it consistently here.
STEP 3 - D. P(growth < 1.7) = 0.42. P(core < 2.0) = 0.70 x 0.10 + 0.30 x 0.42 = 0.196 - the all-38 aggregate almost cannot print below 2.0% with Turkey and Mexico in it, which is why D is crushed relative to the intuitive "capex bust" story. Positive correlation factor 1.3: P(D) = 0.42 x 0.196 x 1.3 = 0.107 -> 11.
STEP 4 - B RESIDUAL = 100 - 11 - 28 - 11 = 50.
CONSISTENCY CHECK AGAINST CQ2. My CQ2 is 50, driven by a 0.75 marginal on OECD core >= 2.50% over 2027-2036. A 0.486 probability on the stricter >= 2.70% over the narrower 2032-2036 window is coherent with that (higher bar, shorter window, same construction artefact). If I had scored CQ2's inflation conjunct at a Germany-weighted ~0.45, C would fall to ~0.17 and B would rise to ~0.61 - I state this as the explicit sensitivity.
RESIDUAL-B ABSORPTION QUANTIFIED (lens requirement). B's literal band is growth 1.7-2.5%/yr, which carries only ~0.28-0.30 of my growth mass. B's assigned 0.50 therefore absorbs ~20-22 pp that a naive reader would have placed elsewhere, in two identifiable cells: (i) growth < 1.7% with core between 2.0% and 2.7% - approximately 0.42 x 0.32 = ~13-14 pp - satisfies NO literal definition and a naive reader files it under D; (ii) growth between 2.0% and 2.6% with core >= 2.7% - approximately ~8 pp - is a stagflationary outcome that the lock sends to B because step 2 requires growth < 2.0, and a naive reader files it under C. Net: naive D is overstated by ~13-14 pp and naive C by ~8 pp relative to the lock. A reader who scored this without the lock would plausibly report something like A 12 / B 30 / C 33 / D 25; the lock mechanically moves ~20 pp into B.

hypothesis_critique.a: 'SMOOTHLY' carries the failure, and 'supply' carries a second one. The plank asserts a transfer across three non-transferable dimensions at once: occupational (a displaced 45-year-old middle manager in ISIC M is not a licensable care worker - CNA/HCA/Pflege credentialing is 6 months to 3 years and gated by clinical placement capacity, itself staff-constrained), geographic (displacement concentrates in metropolitan service hubs; care shortfalls are worst in non-metro and in Japan/Korea/Southern Europe), and WAGE-LEVEL (Q median hourly pay sits well below J/K/M - the transfer requires accepting a large real pay cut, so in practice the margin clears through migration and through older-worker and second-earner entry, not through white-collar reallocation). My accounting objection is the arithmetic: OECD elder-care FTE shortfalls are counted in millions of positions, while AI white-collar 'savings' show up first as reduced HIRING of entrants, not as released experienced workers - the released stock is far smaller than the gross displacement headline and is in the wrong countries. Also, as a measurement point, if the transfer DID happen it would register as falling Q median wages (low-wage entrant surge), so the plank's success would look like failure in the data.
hypothesis_critique.b: 'BLOCKS' carries the failure; 'SEVERELY' carries the second. The plank collapses the two channels the scope lock explicitly separates. AI substitutes for a SUBSET of the VIRTUAL channel - voice BPO, tier-1 support, basic transcription/coding - while PHYSICAL labour migration is COMPLEMENTARY to OECD aging and is accelerating through dedicated care and trade visa routes (Japan SSW, German Pflege/Fachkraefte, UK/Canada care and trades streams, Gulf). The Philippines' physical channel (remittances, ~$38-40B/yr, broad-based) is larger and more demographically protected than its IT-BPM revenue; India's exposure is concentrated in the low-value end while AI raises output per engineer in the high end and India retains the global capability-centre build. 'Blocks' is false as stated: the aggregate labour-export channel widens even as one sub-channel narrows. 'Severely' then fails on magnitude - the realistic outcome is a composition shift inside services exports with a 1-3 year adjustment in margins and entry-level hiring, not a severe national-income shock. Resolution-mechanics note: Philippine IT-BPM headcount is self-reported by the industry association (IBPAP), not a statistical agency, so the first evidence of 'severe' damage will arrive through a lobbied series.
hypothesis_critique.c: 'THEN' carries the failure - the implied sequencing - with 'FALLS' close behind. The plank's structure (hot now, cool later) is exactly what my CQ2 and CQ6 analysis contradicts for the measured aggregate: the GDP-weighted OECD-38 core object keeps a persistent +0.5 to +1.0 pp wedge from its high-inflation members, and the coupled structural forces (grid and care and construction bottlenecks, fiscal dominance with net interest heading to 3% of GDP, labour-force shrinkage) are 2030s phenomena, not 2020s phenomena. There is also no stated referent: 'inflation' is unspecified as to index, aggregate and weighting, so the plank is not falsifiable until a series is named - and the choice of series flips it. The one way it is right: a genuine CQ6-D capex bust with a demand shortfall delivers exactly the hot-then-cold shape, which is why I do not score it near zero.
hypothesis_critique.d: 'EVENTUALLY' carries the failure, and 'WINS' makes it unfalsifiable. 'Eventually' places the claim outside the Dec 31 2036 resolution horizon, so as a resolvable proposition it is empty; and 'wins' names no threshold, no measure and no counterfactual (wins against what - zero growth, the pre-aging trend, per-capita or aggregate?). On substance, the plank asserts that an exponential in ONE input overcomes a decline in another, which is precisely what Jones/Baumol weakest-link elasticities forbid: when output requires many complementary tasks and AI automates a subset, the shadow prices of the non-automated complements rise and CAP aggregate growth - here interconnection and transformer queues, licensed electrician and lineworker hours, and licensed care hours. Those complements are themselves demographically shrinking, so AI capability growth and the binding constraint are negatively coupled. My CQ3 P50 of 1.85% with a P90 of only 2.65% is the quantitative statement that the cap binds through 2036. 'Real GDP' also quietly helps the plank through measurement - hedonic deflation of compute and the capitalization of software and data inflate measured real output without the complements easing.

key_drivers: INDEX-CONSTRUCTION DOMINANCE OF THE INFLATION QUESTIONS: a GDP-weighted (PPP) OECD-38 core aggregate necessarily includes Turkey (~3.5-4%), Mexico (~3.5%), Poland (~2%) and other high-inflation members, adding roughly +0.5 to +1.0 pp versus the G7-weighted mental model. This single fact sets CQ2 at 50 rather than ~32 and sets CQ6-C at 28 rather than ~17, and it is the largest lever in my entire payload.

CHINA'S PPP WEIGHT TIMES ITS AGING DRAG IS THE CQ3 ANSWER: at the locked constant-2025 PPP basis China is ~35% of (OECD-38 + China), so the locked -2.7 pp/yr China aging drag contributes -0.95 pp to the coupled aggregate - essentially the whole locked global -1.1 pp figure. Fixed 2025 weights (no chain-weighting) suppress China's rising share, and the NBS deflator/smoothing bias means the number that RESOLVES sits ~0.25-0.40 pp above the truth.

JONES/BAUMOL WEAKEST-LINK CAP VIA THE GRID AND CARE QUEUES: AI-Q3's P50 of ~998 TWh implies ~350-500 GW of generation plus firming and ~$1.8-2.8T of capex drawn from a demographically shrinking construction and electrical trade pool. The shadow price of interconnection, transformer and licensed-hour complements rises, capping CQ3's P90 at 2.65% regardless of model capability - and pushing probability from CQ6-A into CQ6-B and C.

COMPOSITION EFFECTS INVERT THE SIGN OF THE CQ1 WAGE TEST: a low-wage entrant surge into ISIC Q (and migrant-fed entry into F) drags those MEDIANS down while incumbents gain, and AI truncation of entry-level roles in J/K/M mechanically RAISES those medians. The most AI-disrupted world produces the measured gap in the wrong direction, which is why CQ1's second conjunct is 0.17 and not ~0.35.

SERIES NON-EXISTENCE AND PUBLICATION LAG AS A PROBABILITY SINK: no OECD-38 sectoral real median hourly wage aggregate exists (Eurostat SES is quadrennial with a 3-4 year release lag, so the 2036 endpoint is unobservable at resolution); no official GDP-weighted OECD-38 core aggregate exists; the G7 real-yield construction is not cleanly computable for Italy, Canada and Japan. Unresolvable-as-written conjuncts default toward NO or void, which is a systematic downward force on CQ1 and CQ5.

EQUITY-BOND CORRELATION REGIME AND THE JAPAN DAMPENER: whether the flight-to-quality bid fails depends on the trigger type (inflation/fiscal/basis-trade versus demand shock), and the G7 GDP-weighted 10y nominal aggregate includes a structurally pinned JGB at ~11% PPP weight, which damps the measured rally and makes CQ5's 'fail to fall by 50 bp' conjunct materially easier than it reads.

hypothesis_critique.a: The failing word is 'smoothly', and behind it 'supply'. The plank needs a flow identity to hold across four non-negotiable wedges: occupational (a displaced paralegal is not a licensed CNA), licensing and credentialing (1-2 years plus clinical hours, and the licence is jurisdiction-bound), geographic (the cognitive job losses are metropolitan, the care deficit is dispersed and rural), and wage-level (care pay sits below the reservation wage of the displaced white-collar worker, which is exactly why the administered price has to jump before any reallocation happens at all). Note that 'smoothly' is doing double duty: it smuggles in both a quantity claim and a timing claim, and the timing claim fails even where the quantity claim eventually holds. I score it 6 rather than Wave 1's 5-7 for the same reason they did, so this is the one plank where I have no quarrel with them.
hypothesis_critique.b: The failing word is 'blocks', with 'severely' as the accomplice. AI compresses ONE of two export channels — the virtual one, voice BPO and routine code — while 2A's locked demographics are a direct demand pull on the PHYSICAL one. The Philippines' export earnings lean on nurses, caregivers and seafarers, not only on IT-BPO, and an OECD running a 39-41% old-age ratio with care wages being forced up by budget cycles is the strongest migration-demand configuration in the postwar record. 'Blocks' asserts a closed gate where the evidence shows one gate narrowing and a second widening. India's case is also mis-specified: the GCC/capability-centre model has been absorbing displaced offshore seat count by moving up the task ladder. My 10 is below Wave 1's 12-17 precisely because my coupled world has tighter OECD labour and a stronger physical pull.
hypothesis_critique.c: The failing word is 'falls' — the plank gets the SEQUENCE backwards, not just the level. My structure says 2027-2031 is the disinflationary stretch (capex digestion, post-impairment excess capacity, the AI-Q4 event landing) and 2032-2036 is the re-acceleration (care and trades unit labour costs, grid and electricity pass-through, retiree dissaving, net interest at 3% of GDP tilting the authorities' revealed loss function, and above all the all-38 index composition that no amount of advanced-economy disinflation can outvote). 'Then' is therefore pointed the wrong way. A secondary failure is 'inflation' unqualified: the plank is unresolvable without naming the aggregate, and the Turkey/Mexico weighting fork is worth more than the entire macro disagreement. 15, below Wave 1's 22-33.
hypothesis_critique.d: Two failing words. 'Eventually' is the pure scope-insensitivity tell: it is unfalsifiable at any horizon and silently replaces the Dec 31 2036 resolution date with an unbounded one, so the plank cannot be scored against this question at all as written. 'Wins' is undefined — wins against what counterfactual, and on whose measured series? 'Exponential' is a third problem: the growth contribution of a technology is bounded by Hulten/Aghion-Jones nominal-share erosion regardless of the capability trajectory, so even an exponential capability path yields a bounded aggregate contribution. I am the most sympathetic of the four panelists on the SUBSTANCE — my CQ3 P50 of 2.25% is 35-40 bp above all three Wave-1 panelists and my regime A is 33 against their 11-19 — but the plank as stated is still bad, and I score the stated plank, not my own thesis. 22.

The level of rates as the mechanical driver of both CQ4 and CQ5: a monotone debt-supply ratchet (3.0 bp per pp on ~+20 pp of G7 debt/GDP = +60 bp), retiree dissaving turning INSIDE the 2032-36 window rather than before it, eroding convenience yields, and Japan normalizing at an 11% weight. That takes CQ4 to 2.50 against Wave 1's 1.95-2.10, and because MOVE is a basis-point index it drags CQ5 conjunct A to 0.58 against their 0.42-0.45.

Fiscal monopsony in care as a political variable rather than a wall: all three Wave-1 panelists treated administered care prices as exogenously sticky, which is the drag/pull asymmetry in its purest form. Observed 2021-2025 (US home-health and nursing wages the fastest-rising of any major sector, driven by Medicaid rate increases in ~40 states) shows administered prices catch up in jumps, and the plank is tested in eleven consecutive budget cycles while the decisive voter becomes 65+. This lifts CQ1 conjunct B from their 0.17-0.22 to 0.30.

wave2.coupling_tension:
I reverse the direction of the Wave-1 consensus on the single most important coupling. All three of my Wave-1 panelists concluded that AI-Q1 (23.0% for TFP >= +0.50 pp/yr) is too HIGH once demographics are endogenous — P2 to ~17-18%, P3 to ~18-19%, P1 declining to raise it. I say AI-Q1 is too LOW once demographics are endogenous, and should sit at ~30-33%. Four reasons, each turning a Wave-1 argument against itself. (i) All three marked AI-Q2 (adoption) UP, to 25-30%, on the aging demand pull — correctly — and then claimed the Baumol reweighting channel swallows the output read. P2 computed that channel himself at -0.12 pp/yr. A -0.12 pp drag cannot neutralize a multi-point upward revision in adoption; the arithmetic they supplied does not support the conclusion they drew from it. (ii) TFP is a residual measured against a labour input that is shrinking by construction in 2A. When hours fall and the capital/labour ratio jumps, measured output per hour and the measured residual both rise faster, not slower — endogenizing demographics mechanically HELPS the AI-Q1 numerator. None of the three priced this denominator effect. (iii) The weakest-link cap binds on the LEVEL of bottleneck output, not the growth rate of the aggregate, over a decade in which the bottleneck is 19-23% of GVA against an automatable slice near 45%. (iv) Most importantly, they treated AI-Q4 (impairment) and AI-Q1 (TFP) as substitutes. Coupled, they are COMPLEMENTS: the historical record of capital supercycles is impairment-of-financiers alongside arrival-of-productivity, because the write-down collapses the user cost of the service to its adopters. The joint distribution implied by coupling therefore carries POSITIVE correlation between AI-Q4 and AI-Q1 — the exact opposite sign to the one Wave 1 assumed and the one that 2B's marginal-by-marginal elicitation cannot express at all.
Two further directional tensions. AI-Q3's P50 of 998 TWh is too LOW, not too high: P1 cut it to 850-900 on cost of capital and P2 cut the P90 to 1,350 on electrician scarcity, but datacenter load is set by the compute price and the willingness-to-pay ceiling as a share of GDP, and my GDP path is ~35-40 bp/yr stronger than theirs while China — 35% of the block and the fastest grid builder on record — faces no interconnection-queue constraint of the US kind. I would centre AI-Q3 nearer 1,100 TWh with the P90 left intact. AI-Q5 (J/K/M compensation share -3.5 pp) is too low at 38.2% and should sit near 50%, for the reason P3 gave and the other two did not: SNA-2008 capitalization of software, data and R&D plus hyperscaler rent booked inside sector J inflate the GVA denominator while shrinking entrant cohorts and entry-level truncation cut the compensation numerator — two mechanical forces, no wage story required.
The honest counter-tension against my own payload: AI-Q5 high and AI-Q1 high together describe a world of real productivity AND concentrated capital income, which is precisely the BIS Box C configuration — output rising while labour income lags. That is the one route by which my high-growth, high-rate, regime-A-heavy distribution is wrong in the direction Wave 1 chose, and it is why I hold D at 5 rather than 2 and keep my CQ3 P10 at 1.20.
